crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
children.blurb: The threshold of machine authorship is the legal line between a work created by a human and one created by a machine, applied to copyright, patent inventorship, and related rights.

children.name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
children.blurb: Autonomous entities are AI systems that can initiate transactions, manage assets, or make binding decisions with limited human intervention.

children.name: Liability When Agents Interact
children.blurb: This page covers legal responsibility when two or more AI agents interact without a human directly approving each step.

children.name: Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards
children.blurb: Deepfakes are synthetic audio, image, or video created or altered by machine learning to depict a person saying or doing something they did not.

children.name: The Right to an Explanation
children.blurb: The right to an explanation concerns whether a person affected by an automated decision can obtain a meaningful account of how that decision was reached.

sections.body: Emerging legal frameworks is the study of how courts, legislatures, and regulators are responding to artificial intelligence systems that create, act, and produce evidence. Right now, AI is generating text, images, music, and code that people try to register or protect as intellectual property, and courts are deciding whether a human must be involved for a work to be owned. AI systems are also being used to draft contracts, manage assets, and make decisions, which raises questions about who is responsible when the system acts without direct human control. In litigation, lawyers and courts are dealing with fabricated or altered media, and some jurisdictions are writing rules that require a person to be told why an automated decision was made. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows how much of this work is happening in real disputes rather than in theory.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Machine authorship has produced a few early decisions and 29 AI case law precedents, but there is no settled rule across countries about whether an AI can be an author or inventor. Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries are mostly experimental; no legal system has fully recognized an AI as a person or trustee, and liability for multi-agent interactions is still being worked out case by case. Deepfake evidence is a live problem because detection tools are not reliable enough for courts to rely on alone, and many rules of evidence were written before this technology existed. The right to an explanation exists in some privacy and AI laws, but what counts as a meaningful explanation is still contested. Honest limits include the fact that 6,825 state AI bills are tracked, but most have not become law, and the 210 compliance and regulation pages reflect a patchwork rather than a coherent framework.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with The Threshold of Machine Authorship to understand the basic question of whether a machine can create a protected work, because that issue underlies many intellectual property disputes. Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries then moves from creation to action, explaining what happens when an AI is given authority over money or decisions. Liability When Agents Interact builds on that by looking at what happens when two or more AI systems cause harm together, which is where multi-agent liability becomes concrete. Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards shifts to the courtroom and the rules for proving that a video, image, or audio recording is real. The Right to an Explanation closes the section by asking what a person is owed when an AI system makes a decision about them, connecting the earlier pages on action and liability to individual rights.
